title: The Tradition of Dussehra and the Historical Evolution of Ravan‐Dahan in Indian Sanatan Dharma: A Historical and Cultural Study from Ancient Religious Beliefs to Modern Public Celebrations
content: Background: Vijayadashami, commonly known as Dussehra, holds a prominent place in the religious, social, and cultural calendar of the Indian Sanatan tradition. While the defining feature of its celebration in North and Central India today is 'Ravan-dahan' the public burning of the colossal effigies of Ravana, Kumbhakarna, and Meghnada, accompanied by fireworks ancient texts suggest that this tradition is relatively recent. In reality, it is a practice superimposed upon much older Vedic, Puranic, martial, and agrarian traditions. Methods: This study adopted a qualitative methodology that combined historical comparison with textual hermeneutics. It examines primary sources in Sanskrit and vernacular languages—such as the Rigveda, Atharvaveda, Valmiki Ramayana, Devi Mahatmya (from the Markandeya Purana), Kalika Purana, Arthashastra, Raghuvamsa, and Tulsidas’s Ramcharitmanas. Furthermore, it incorporates medieval royal chronicles, colonial ethnographic accounts (such as James Tod’s 'Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan' and James Prinsep’s observations on Banaras), as well as contemporary cultural-sociological studies. Results: Its historical development encompasses four distinct phases:-(i) Following the monsoon, Vedic seasonal sacrifices (sharad anushthana) and royal military expeditions (simollanghana and ayudha puja) were conducted(ii) Within Shakta traditions, the victory of Goddess Durga over the demon Mahishasura was incorporated into the observance of Ashvina Shukla Dashami (iii) In the sixteenth century, bhakti (devotional) traditions brought the narrative of Rama to the masses through Ramlila. This practice was initiated by Goswami Tulsidas and supported by the Maharaja of Banaras in Ramnagar;(iv) Between the nineteenth and twenty-first centuries, the custom of burning effigies evolved into an urban public event. This transformation accelerated following the Partition of 1947, as refugees arriving from Punjab and North India helped establish the practice in Delhi and its surrounding regions. Subsequently, the widespread influence of television and digital culture further shaped this tradition. Conclusions: The burning of Ravana is neither mentioned in the Vedas nor is it a part of Valmiki’s original epic; rather, it evolved within the Ramlila tradition as an audio-visual pedagogical tool. Over time, it became linked to royal Dussehra celebrations and, in the post-independence era, to civic nationalism. This multi-dimensional process of evolution illustrates how Sanatan Dharma through vibrant public rituals continuously generates new interpretations of ancient spiritual symbols, such as the triumph of Dharma (righteousness) over adharma (unrighteousness).
